utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today, we are Wednesday, the 7th of May, 2008. I'd like to welcome the representatives of the Prosecution, the witness, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us in the courtroom. We need to resume the examination-in-chief conducted by the Prosecution of the witness. We are in open session. I would like to tell the Prosecution that it has 45 minutes left, approximately, to complete its examination-in-chief, but we can check with the Registrar and look at the countdown. You have the floor for the end of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, you mentioned yesterday that Capalo was one of Stanko Vujanovic's men. Could you give us Capalo's first and last name, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojnovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Vujanovic"] is his last name, and his name is Mirko, I think. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, we mentioned the possible connections between --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just checking to see whether the witness's microphone was on. Could you repeat your answer, please, or the comment you just made, Witness 002, as regards the first and last name of Capalo?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, the witness is speaking English, so there is no interpretation into English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last name is Vojnovic. I think his name is Mirko. So it's not Vujanovic, as it said in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday, when we discussed the possible connections between Stanko Vujanovic and the Serbian Radical Party, on page T6514, line 6 to 9 of the transcript, you mentioned that you didn't know what connections there were between Stanko Vujanovic and the SDS before the war. If you like, I'd like to remind you of something you stated previously, and I'm referring here to the recorded interview which took place last Sunday, on the 4th of May, 2008. On page 12 of the transcript, on the third tape, page 12 in B/C/S, the recording bears number T001-1596. There is a B/C/S version that has been uploaded into e-court. The 65 ter of this is 7221. 7221 is the 65 ter number of the version that has been uploaded on e-court, 7221, page 74. We don't have the transcript of this in English, but I have the corresponding excerpt in front of me, and I suggest I read it. So let me start off: [In English] "Let's target the period between 1990 and 1991. I mean from September to November 1991 to 1992. How did you see Seselj at the time period; if you have any recollection?"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask the Prosecutor to identify the page for me in Serbian. Page 12, there is no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is on page 12 of the third tape, which is in document 65 ter number 7221, page 74 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the best would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought Mr. Seselj had a hard copy version of this, but if he doesn't, maybe we could display it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have the document in your language before you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that there's something wrong with the methodology. I found this page 12 now, but I'm not quite sure that I've found the passage that is quoted by counsel for the Prosecution. But as for the methodology that the Prosecutor is using, there is something wrong. He should be putting questions to the witness, so then if the witness doesn't know what to say, in terms of what the Prosecutor is expecting him to say, then the Prosecutor can jog his memory, not to offer an answer in advance. I don't think this is right. If you've read the transcript, there are a lot of leading questions. It's called running the gauntlet in our country, that is to say, running the gauntlet, being beaten from all sides. It seems to me that this witness ran through a gauntlet during the interview on Sunday, beaten from all sides. So since he does not dare put leading questions here in the courtroom, then he is showing this piece of paper, where there were so many leading questions. I think that the Prosecutor should put questions to the witness properly. I don't mind having his memory jogged, but I'm saying this as a matter of principle. I don't see anything troublesome for me, in my own position, in this transcript anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, I don't have the original question in front of me, but if I understood correctly, your approach, following a question that was put, the witness answered in a certain way, and you realised that his answer did not square with something which you were made aware of in the past, namely, last Sunday. And therefore you would like to jog his memory by reminding him that last Sunday, when asked the same question on the same topic, you put the question to him and he gave such-and-such an answer. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir, absolutely. The question has not been phrased exactly the same way, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the answer he gave previously does not coincide with the answer we have on the screen. Therefore, you wish to jog his memory. So, basically, you are refreshing his memory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me resume. Let me start from the beginning again. Question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which line of the text are you talking about, in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S, this is on line -- I shall give it to you straight away, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have numbers here, and the numbers run from 1 to 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall tell you very soon. 19, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19. Thank you. Mr. Seselj, please turn to line 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall start reading this excerpt: [In English] "Let's target the period between 1991. I mean from September to November from 1991 to 1992." "How did you see Seselj at the time period, if you have any recollection?" "At the moment when this happened in 1991, I saw him as a great leader." "Do you remember whether you were the only one who saw him as a great leader among the volunteers, fighting on the Serbian side, whether others saw him as you did or --" "I believe that the complete Territorial Defence was delighted because he came."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, this was not referred to at all. Now the -- why would the Prosecutor remind the witness of something that he hadn't questioned him about at all on the previous day? Yesterday, he asked about Stanko Vujanovic, and the witness said that Stanko Vujanovic, after the war, joined the Serb Radical Party. That is an undeniable fact. Stanko Vujanovic was a candidate of this party in the elections in Republika Srpska Krajina in 1993 and became an MP. That is an undeniable fact. However, now he is reminding him how to describe my arrival and the impression I left on the soldiers, volunteers, et cetera. Why doesn't he put a direct question to him? Perhaps that's exactly what the witness is going to say. Perhaps he's going to put it in even nicer terms. This has not been contested at all so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the questions put relate to the way in which the volunteers saw Mr. Seselj, so we have questions and answers. Then Mr. Seselj says this is all very well, but this topic could have been addressed without refreshing the memory of the witness directly. So why are you addressing this issue now, Mr. Dutertre?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are a few lines put in context which will enable us to better understand the period in question. We are better able to put the witness's answer into perspective as regards the question, namely, the connection between Stanko Vujanovic and the SRS. This is to put it in context and understand the answer of the witness in chronological terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, you wish to refresh the witness's memory because -- just a minute, Mr. Seselj. I will give you the floor, but I'm trying to summarise all of this. I think the issue raised as is follows: A previous question was put to Mr. Stankovic [as interpreted] on the possible connection between Stanko Vujanovic and the SRS. The Prosecution has a problem with the date and the period, and this is what the Prosecution would like to highlight. And the Prosecution acknowledges that the answers of the witness do not enable it to properly understand the time frame. Therefore, Mr. Dutertre is jogging his memory to raise issues which were -- questions which were put to the witness last Sunday relating to Mr. Seselj, and in this manner the Prosecution will be able to put this in the right time period in order to establish the possible connections between Mr. Stanko Vujanovic and the SRS. Maybe I got this wrong, but this is how I have understood all of this. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this has to do with the witness's description of my arrival in Vukovar and going to the frontline, to the absolute line of fire. He testifies here on a great many pages how I impressed everyone. I was moving in the middle of the street, whereas my escorts were by the houses. I thrilled these people. Then there is a leading question: "Can one conclude on the basis of that that you admired him, adored him?" At the end of page 12. What does "adore" mean? We Serbs don't do that kind of thing. Living persons are not adored. I think that the witness should answer questions here. The Prosecutor wants to ask him about my visit and the impression I left, and then perhaps once he describes this, then the Prosecutor can ask additional questions, but now he's reminding him of something that hadn't been referred to at all. Stanko Vujanovic was an episode yesterday. There was a leading question about his contacts with the Serb Radical Party. I intervened and I said that that question was not put in the right way, you have to ask whether such a thing happened and from when. And then the witness said that Stanko Vujanovic joined the Serb Radical Party after the war. That was the only reference to Stanko Vujanovic. There was nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could the speakers please be asked to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer now mentioned comes straight after this excerpt I've just been reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, just let's see and wait until the end of the questions, and, Mr. Seselj, you can protest again, but you're protesting when we don't even have all the information. This makes it difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I shall resume the reading of this document: [In English] "And what could one conclude from that? It is just a question. That because you have this kind of adoration for him, that he would have moral influence over you and the members of the Territorial Defence?" "It had influence on the leaders of the Territorial Defence. Stanko Vujanovic joined the Radical Party after that. For them, it was such a big propaganda." "When you said 'them,' what did you mean?" "The Radicals." "What do you mean by this? The visit of Seselj to Vukovar or after that?" "I think his visit to Vukovar." [Interpretation] This is the end of the excerpt I wanted to read, and I was going to put my question to the witness. I wanted to ask him whether he remembers having stated this during the interview we had with him last Sunday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I protest again, because I think this is highly inappropriate and impermissible. There is yet another sentence where the witness says: "I think that by virtue of the fact that he visited Vukovar, this was a major advantage. And in the following months, had there been a vote in Vukovar, he would have won about 95 per cent of the vote for sure." I am not trying to side-step anything the witness said on Sunday. It has to do with my role. But that was not referred to in the examination-in-chief. The Prosecutor should first put a question and then let the witness answer, and then ask additional questions. Now he's reading out to him what it was that he said on Sunday and then putting questions. That is impermissible, Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This exchange of views, this is the conclusion I draw: Mr. Stanko Vujanovic was not a member of the Serbian Radical Party before the arrival of Mr. Seselj, and according to the witness, it seems he joined afterwards. I think this is an interesting piece of information. Maybe this is not what the Prosecution is aiming at, but it's nonetheless an interesting piece of information. You may resume your question. So, Witness 002, this is what you stated last Sunday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question to put to you, Witness. It seems that in light of this exchange of views, that one of the fighters from Vukovar, who seemingly was part of a unit, a so-called volunteers unit, was not a member of the SRS before the arrival of Mr. Seselj. Therefore, among all your comrades who were volunteers, as far as you know, were there volunteers predominantly affiliated to the SRS or were they in a minority, or is it something you don't know, because last Sunday, 15 years after the events, you say, "Well, this person joined afterwards." So maybe you have a clear understanding of political issues, and you if you have this particular knowledge, I would tend to ask you this question: Those people that were with you, those people who were by the car -- we could see this picture again. When I saw this picture, this is a question that came to mind. All these people on the photograph, were they all members of the SRS or weren't they, or were some of them members, or were they all members, or were they predominantly SRS members? What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for these people by the car, as far as I know, at that point none of them were members of the Serb Radical Party. They told me about some liberals, whatever, something meaningless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please don't quote any names, because we are in open session. You have just told us something which is important, and on reading the transcript in English, you say, "None of them were members of the Serbian Radical Party." Do you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say what my opinion is. I cannot give any guarantees. I think they were not. None of them had told me that they were members of the Serb Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that I really have to intervene. The witness told you that they were talking about liberals. This has to do with Montenegrins. This liberal party is from Montenegro. I had to intervene. I think that you should register the witness's entire answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj was addressing another issue. Now, who are these liberals, as far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, I was an apolitical person before the war. I was just interested in Serb nationalism. I wasn't interested in politics, as such. I didn't want to be a member of any party, because I had my own views on Serbdom. So I am not familiar with these liberals. I know that there are some liberals, but what this is all about, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question for you, relating to this matter. We have heard a number of testimonies in this courtroom, and from these I had understood that some volunteers had been recruited by the Serbian Radical Party, which -- and these people were not members of the SRS. Since the question relates to the issue of recruiting these volunteers, I would like you to clarify this for us, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look. As far as I know, I mean, this recruitment of volunteers in Serbia was carried out by the Serb Radical Party, by Vuk Draskovic's party and Jovic's party, too. I forget his first name now. They all send their volunteers either to Croatia or to Bosnia. Since the Judge strictly asked me about the persons by the car, they came of their own free will. No one had recruited them. So I really do not know whether they were members of a party. They talked to me about some liberals, but since I was not a political person, I wasn't interested in that at all. I was interested in fighting. I was not interested at all in whether this fight for Serbdom fit into some political plan or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But to your knowledge, were volunteers recruited by the SRS in a position not to be members of the SRS; was it possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, I think it was. It was like this: The unit that arrived and that was under the command of Kameni, as far as I know, they had all been mobilised by the Serbian Radical Party, to the best of my knowledge. So that unit was formed in Sid, and unless I'm very much mistaken, that was around the 16th of October somewhere. And from Sid, it was sent, under Kameni's command, to Vukovar. But that unit had nothing to do with what the Judge asked about the territorials. They're not the same people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we're talking about Stankovic [as interpreted] again here. You stated he became a member of the Serbian Radical Party after Mr. Seselj's visits. In your recollection, did he join the SRS the day after Mr. Seselj's visit or did he join the SRS during the war that followed? What clarification can you give us about this? Did it happen the following day, later on, during the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm sorry to interrupt. There might be a mistake in the translation. Page 13, line 9, I see the name of "Stankovic." I don't know if we are really talking about the same person, because I thought I understood something else in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm talking about Stanko Vujanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another objection, Mr. President. I'm not challenging that you have the right to leading questions, as a Judge, but I have to remind you that yesterday the witness said quite precisely, and this must be in the transcript, that Stanko Vujanovic became a member of the Serbian Radical Party after the war, after the war. That's what the witness stated yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely, we need to know whether it happened after the war, because after the war, when Vukovar fell, we can say that the war was over in Vukovar. That's why I'm asking the question again, because this needs to be clarified. And my question was not a leading question, that's all; it was an open question. He had the choice to answer whichever way he liked. It's not a leading question, because you answer by "yes" or "no" to a leading question, whereas he had three choices to answer my question. So I refute what you have just said. Sir, the question is the following: This Stanko Vujanovic, to your knowledge, when exactly did he join the SRS? Apparently he was not a member of the SRS before Mr. Seselj's visit. Now, when exactly did he join? Well, you know it or you don't know it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, let me say that I don't know exactly when he became a member. Secondly, I have certain assumptions. As far as I know Stanko Vujanovic, I can make assumptions. I was disillusioned, personally, with the radical party when I heard that Stanko Vujanovic had become a radical, and that was sometime in 1992 already, because I considered that he was not the right person, a person valuable enough to be a member of any political party, and that he was just toppling the authority of the party by joining it. So I don't really know. I think that that is something that can be proved through the Court. Mr. Seselj can show a membership card for Stanko Vujanovic, and then you can see when exactly he did become a member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure that Mr. Seselj will have no problem to establish this. But through the question put to you by my fellow Judge, a new problem has arisen, and I'm going to try and clarify this with you. My fellow Judge mentioned the issue of volunteers recruitment, and you stated that politicians, including Mr. Seselj, but he was not the only one, you stated that politicians were recruiting volunteers. These volunteers were then sent on to various front lines or other places. Listening to your answer, the following question came to my mind. I was wondering if the politicians at the time were calling people -- calling on people to join the armed forces, to fight, but without necessarily saying, "Join my party." They were just saying, maybe, "Please join the fight for our country, for our values," but without necessarily telling the people, "You should join the SRS," or any other party. Talking about this recruitment process, and you are an educated man, you went to university, I'm sure you understand the meaning of my question, was this political kind of recruitment to call people to join a political party and then to send them to fight, or are we talking about recruitment in the larger meaning of the word, for these people to go and fight? Do you understand the difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see a nuance there, or, rather, I can give you my own personal opinion about that. What I consider is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in your own personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally feel that not only Mr. Seselj but the other two, Vuk Draskovic and Jovic, that in fact they were scoring political points, because at the time Serb nationalism was expanding in Serbia, and also because they collected up volunteers for the war in Croatia and Bosnia, and by doing so they scored major political points in Serbia, specifically. That's my own opinion. It was a political promotion, rather than the fact of sending volunteers as being a military factor of any kind. I personally think that the Army of Yugoslavia could have done without the assistance of the Serb volunteers, done what it did without them. That's my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just added something, and it's quite significant. You're telling us that the JNA could have conducted that recruitment. We've heard several witnesses tell us that the JNA was conducting operations that may have not have been in line with the wishes of the population, because apparently from what we heard, the JNA was connected to the former communist regime and the population, the citizens, some of them did not want -- by joining the JNA, did not want to give the impression that they wanted to support the old system. Therefore, they preferred to join as volunteers to distance themselves from the JNA. That's what we heard. I don't know if it's true or not, but what do you think about this, yourself? And I'm putting that question to you because you raised that issue, saying that the JNA could have done that work. Considering what you've just said, I'm just sharing with you what other witnesses told us and who explained why the JNA was not in a position -- could not do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this: First of all, the Guards Brigade, when it arrived in Vukovar, it could have taken the town in a single day. That's an indisputable fact. People can say what they like, but they could have done that. Now, as far as the recruitment goes, it was like this: The Croatian forces at the time might have had some 100.000 soldiers - I don't believe they had that much, but let's put that as a maximum number. In Serbia, in 1991, there were 130.000 officers, professional soldiers, well trained, so they didn't have to recruit anybody else. They had enough men for all officers armed, to go to Croatia, and win the war without a single soldier. That's what I meant, and that's what I thought when I said that the Yugoslav People's Army didn't need volunteers, and as far as the recruitment is concerned. Now, the problem of recruitment was what it was because every person who had done its military service had in their military booklet its recruitment location, that should a mobilisation break out, they would know where to go, but the problem is with the following, and I can quote my own example. At the time, I officially lived in Vukovar, but as I was studying I was actually in Novi Sad. And in military booklet my recruitment post was Vinkovci, which was at the time under Croatian authority, and in case of a mobilisation, I would have to report to the Croats, for example, at this mobilisation post. So directly report to the enemy, in fact, for mobilisation. So this was totally absurd and you couldn't apply the law, by the same token, and you have to understand that there was complete disarray in our country at the time. Quite simply, the law could not have been applied strictly, and you had to deviate from the law constantly. So that was a problem. I was not able to report and join up with the army. When I went to the barracks, they told me to report to my mobilisation post, which was absolutely absurd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. With respect to the military booklet, and that's a matter we dealt at length with a number of witnesses, when you were sent to the Guards Brigade, did you give them your military booklet and did they stamp that military booklet with a stamp from the Guards Brigade? You are telling us that normally you should have gone to Croatia, but because of chaos, that was not possible. So when you joined the Guards Brigade, did you give them your military booklet for them to stamp it and to acknowledge that you were indeed a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I gave them my military booklet. First of all, I didn't have it with me, my military booklet with me, and that was one of the problems. And, secondly, I don't think anybody asked me for my military booklet. I had a certificate -- or, rather, I had a bus ticket which confirmed that I had arrived in Sid as a volunteer, and -- I really can't remember what happened with the booklet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This allows clarification on some other issues related to the military booklet. Mr. Dutertre, sorry for this interruption, but we needed to clarify these points. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe that I have about 40 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, you mentioned the SRS detachment set up in Sid, under the leadership of Kameni. What was the first -- what were the first and last name of Kameni?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is a classical example of where the Prosecutor does have the right to remind the witness and jog his memory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, Mr. Seselj is coming to your help. Tell him the name. Is it Milan Lancuzanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When the SRS detachment, with Kameni at its head, arrived in Vukovar, how were these men dressed? What type of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had camouflage uniforms. As far as I know, new ones. And we were a little jealous of them, because we had some old uniforms which were in pretty bad shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know who had given them these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I assume that since they had arrived as a detachment of the Serbian Radical Party, I assumed that it was the Serbian Radical Party which provided the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to fight side by side with them when you were in Vukovar until November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did have parallel actions, not directly joint actions but parallel actions. We would be in one street, they would be in the street next-door. Or, rather, at one point we did have an action in the same street when Mr. Seselj arrived. We went on the left-hand side, and the members of the Radical Party or that detachment were on the opposite side of the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. You remember the names of some of the members of this SRS detachment with whom you may have conducted parallel if not joint operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember the nicknames of a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you give them to us, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kina, Belgija, Ceca. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who is the individual nicknamed "Mali Joe"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were two more guys. One was Mali Joe, and the other one was Veliki Joe. Little Joe and Big Joe. One was very short, 1 metre 55, 56; and the other one, Big Joe, was almost 2 metres tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. Which unit did Mali Joe belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was also in the detachment of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What was the reputation, as far as you know? What was the reputation as fighters of Kina, Belgija, Mali Joe; what was their reputations as fighters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As fighters, it was good. The only thing is that I assumed that they engaged in criminal activity before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And with respect to Ceca [Realtime transcript read in error "Cica"], what do you know about his reputation as a fighter? Ceca.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have absolutely no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: My question was related to Ceca, spelled C-e-c-a and not C-i-c-a as can be read at page 21, line 3 of the transcript. Who is the individual nicknamed "Topola"? Maybe it's his first name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was some sort of Serb volunteer. I -- I'm not quite sure whether I can tell you in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, who is the individual nicknamed Tap?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tap? During the war, he was about 14 years old, 13 or 14. He was a member, I assume, of the Territorial Defence. He was killed two or three years after the liberation in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know if there was a connection between him and Kameni?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he constantly -- he was with Kameni all the time after the war. He would be seen around with him all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know who is the individual nicknamed Cedo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a lot of people. I really don't know. I'd have to see his photograph to be able to tell you for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You're saying that it could be a lot of people, but do you have anybody in mind? Could you tell us about these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: The Croats would say "Cede," "Cedo," when referring to Chetnik, as a term of endearment, but you can also have a man's name, it can also be a male name. So until I see the photograph, I can't really know who it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. Let me move on to a completely different topic. After having had a look at the structure of the SRS unit and of the TO, let me now move on to Ovcara and the 20th of November. You stated that you were there. My question is the following: With whom did you go to Ovcara, with which one of your fellow fighters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we're in open session. Do you want to answer in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You mentioned a gauntlet and you said that the prisoners walked through this gauntlet. After that, where were they asked to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would enter the hangar directly after running through the gauntlet, so the gauntlet was actually connecting the bus and the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How many prisoners were there in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't count them. It was between 200 to 400. I heard from someone that there were 372, but I really don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In what physical condition were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in a bad state, because they had -- they were beaten before they actually entered the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Which members of the TO or volunteers did you see in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Djankovic in the hangar. Later, I saw Jovica Peric. At one point at the end, I saw Tap and little Zoric. I really cannot recall anyone else right now. I think it's all there in my statement, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes, but the Bench would like to hear what you have to say orally. This is why I'm putting this question to you, so that you can shed some light on this. Miroljub Vujovic, was he in the hangar? Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He came to the hangar because of a situation there. It was forbidden to shoot in the hangar, in order not to frighten the prisoners who were in the hangar, and Djani at one time fired in order to frighten a prisoner next to him, and Miroljub came to tell him that he mustn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone you knew in the hangar? I mean amongst the victims, not the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognised about 50 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Would you be able to - I know this happened a long time ago - to give us any names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember right now, but when the investigator showed me photographs, I showed him exactly who were the people that I saw in the hangar. So there is a list of names there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you see Berghofer and Perkan in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we in closed or private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You mentioned having received a cockade from Mr. Seselj. When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he came to visit Vukovar. I don't remember the exact date. I think this was in November, the 11th, the 12th, or the 13th. I don't remember exactly which date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Which months, which year was this in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And where were you when you received this cockade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I'm not exactly sure, because the houses are right next to each other, but I think this was in the house of Kameni, in the yard of that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Had you seen him elsewhere on that day in Vukovar, before and after?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him. There was a mopping-up action of the Tri Ruze Street, and Mr. Seselj came with an escort to see his fighters in action, because the fighters from the Radical Party Detachment were working the right side of that street, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you've just said, and this is something you mentioned yesterday, you said that the streets needed to be cleaned up. I don't know what the term is exactly in your language, but in French, cleaning up, mopping up, has a very precise meaning. Can you tell me what you mean when you are given the order to mop up? In military terms, what does this stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the military sense, we were supposed to go down the street, to check all the houses, and to take out all the civilians, everything that we had found in the house, and pass them on. Or if we found enemies, we were supposed to push them back or destroy them, depending on the situation. This was a term that we used, and we were not ordered in any way to do anything that would be contrary to the Geneva Conventions. Perhaps a more precise term would be to liberate the street, but we actually used the term "to mop up the street."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said "to contain the enemy." Now, in the following case, let's assume that the enemy surrenders, raises his arms, has no arms anymore, and hands over his arms. What kind of instructions did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, no one had given me any kind of instructions. While I was in the Guards Brigade, the order was that there should be no shooting of those who surrender or those who are unarmed. In the Territorial Defence, no one had said anything to me, so the assumption was that it was the same. I'm speaking on the basis of my personal experience now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the TO Defence hadn't told you anything. Now, when you, together with your comrades, you mopped up the streets, did you take anybody prisoner or were there no prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, for the most part it was Ustashas that were running away, so they did not stay behind to surrender. As for the civilians that we got out of the cellars, we considered them to be civilians, so we did not engage in a procedure of capture. We sent them further on to Velepromet. In fact, my unit did not have a single procedure of capture. Quite simply, no one had surrendered to us during the course of two months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to break now. Mr. Dutertre, I believe you have a few seconds left, unless you've completed your examination-in-chief. Did you have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be grateful if I could have an additional five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you are given an additional five minutes, that will apply to Mr. Seselj as well. The best is probably to have the break now and to give you five minutes when we resume. Mr. Seselj will have an additional five minutes as well. Let's take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, with respect to the SRS detachment, you gave us a number of names, and you stated that you conducted a number of operations alongside them. How would you rate your knowledge of this SRS detachment during the war in Vukovar? In other words, did you know them well or was your knowledge limited? How would you describe your knowledge you had of this detachment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really socialise with them. I don't know. My assumption was that in the past, they had been criminals, something like that, so I had no ambition to socialise with them. As fighters, they were good. I don't remember now exactly that we were in some particular operations together, except for that particular one when Mr. Seselj came.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What was the impact of Mr. Seselj's visit on the TO soldiers and on the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. Seselj was the only politician who came to see us, so we were all thrilled that someone had come to see us. I personally started appreciating Mr. Seselj a lot more after that, because I saw that he cared about his army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: At that time, starting with this visit, what sort of influence did you find that he had on the TO soldiers and on the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I can only talk about what I think as a private person. What the others thought, I don't know, but I can assume. I, personally, was pleased by the borders advocated by Mr. Seselj, because my house was close to those borders. It was logical that I should think that this territory should be Serbia. I assume that other Krajina people were of the same view.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: According to you, what was the extent of his influence on TO members and on volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Questions cannot be put this way, because this witness is not an expert. He can talk about his impressions, about effects. And the Prosecutor is asking him to assess the extent of one's influence. That can only be done by an expert, and not even an expert. This is a fact witness, and questions have to be tailored to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you have the impression, looking at your fellow fighters, that Mr. Seselj was someone people listened to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, if Mr. Seselj had expressed a wish when he came then, we would have certainly played along. If he had asked us to win another three streets, we would have taken those three streets. He was a vojvoda. We would not have refused his order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. If you can answer the following question, because you're not a political expert, but you stated that you're interested in political matters, how would you describe Mr. Seselj's position on the political scene? Was his position important or not? Before the beginning of the war, how would you describe his situation on the political scene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally think that before the war, Mr. Seselj did not have a chance in any election, since as a nationalist, he was brought to the forefront, politically speaking, if I can put it that way, only when there was a need for nationalism; that is to say, when Serbia was threatened from a national point of view. So I believe that if there were a fair democratic election in 1992, Mr. Seselj would have won it. That's my opinion. Now, I really don't know. Had you had a vote in Vukovar after Seselj came there, he would have won by a landslide.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You stated that you were given a cockade by Mr. Seselj. Could you describe it for us, that cockade? We saw a rather unclear picture of it on your hat, but could you give us a detailed description of that cockade, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cockade is a double-headed eagle with a skull and crossed bones. It's a real cockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What group, specifically, did wear that sort of cockade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I am convinced that it's a Chetnik cockade. Now, what the exact formation was in the Second World War that wore it, what Chetnik formation, I really don't know. With this cockade, I considered myself to be a true Chetnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: One last question. By the end of the fighting in Vukovar, were you made aware of incidents that took place at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't have any other question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, with respect to what we've just discussed, but I want you to tell us about the facts you witnessed yourself and nothing else, after Mr. Seselj's visits did you see any changes in the way the SRS volunteers were behaving? Did you see any change in their behaviour during fighting or various operations? Did you notice any change? Did you find that their commitment was stronger? Did you notice that they were more violent or less violent? And I don't want your impressions. I want facts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, I cannot answer your question, because no one had ever asked me that until now, and I never thought about it. Now I'm supposed to remember what the situation was 17 years ago. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not even if you tried to remember something that could have happened after that visit? If we gave you a bit more time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In closed session, I can tell you about a private detail, and I believe that that is why I cannot remember. That will explain to you the reason why it is that I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we'll move into private session to find out about this private detail. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With my questions, I want to address the visits of Mr. Seselj to Vukovar. You stated that you received a cockade after requesting it. We know that you were not a member of the Leva Supoderica unit. You were given a cockade. At the time, you were not a member of the SRS, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never a member of the Serb Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You told us that you received the cockade. That's what I understood, and if I'm mistaken, please tell me so. Well, you told us that you received it because it was the symbol of belonging to the Chetnik movement; is that what you stated? We've heard other witnesses, and some of them told us that they joined the SRS, or that they were volunteers, or that they were Chetniks, and some of them told us that they did so also because they were royalists and that they joined the Chetnik movement for that particular reason. You were in Vukovar. You met other fighters. Did you talk to these soldiers, and did you have the feeling that amongst them, there were royalists who joined the army, who volunteered, because they were maybe fighting for the restoration of the monarchy or with reference to the past?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for the group that was with me, they were some kind of liberals, whatever. We did not discuss politics very much, because I personally, if I can put it this way, am an advocate of the monarchy, and I believe that had a monarchy been introduced in Serbia, many negative things would not have happened, had we had a king. I was not really involved in political discussions during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an interesting piece of information. Now, with respect to the cockade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for cockades, I personally wanted to have a cockade for reasons of tradition, because I believe that my family hails from Herzegovina. It would have meant a great deal to me had I returned there with a cockade and with a decoration, if possible. So these are my personal reasons. I would have been very proud of that, and my family would have been very proud of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the fighters at the time, receiving a cockade, if I understand you explanations, could have not a political meaning, meaning that they belonged to a specific political party, but it could be based on personal considerations. And they might want a cockade also because it might refer to the past, to specific ideas, that's an assumption I'm making, or it might refer, that cockade, or it might represent some sort of recognition for having taken part in military operations? This is a question I would like you to answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, at that time, in my view, the cockade meant that the person wearing a cockade does not want to have anything to do with communism. In the former Yugoslavia, for no reason, Serbia was labelled as the communist side, as opposed to Croatia that was labelled as non-communist or pro-Western. I did not see a special reason for that. However, the cockade, if I can put it this way, meant that we were opposed to communism, meant that we were not communists. It represented something different. Secondly, many Serbs, in their tradition, in their families, before the Second World War, well, there were many families whose men were among the Chetniks, who were always opposed to communism. So my grandmother told me that whenever I talked about Tito, that she talked to me about the king, and she told me that what we were learning at school was not true, that they lived very nicely during the time of the king, and that she was not opposed to the king at all. She did not dare say that she liked him. She got killed during the course of this war, but I really wanted to show up in front of her with this cockade to show that I was also a proponent of something different, compared to what it was that I talked about when I was a little boy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We saw a number of video clips, and the Prosecutor could have shown it as well, with soldiers in Vukovar, and they are wearing JNA helmets, and we also see soldiers with hats and cockades. What you've just said reminds me of these videos we saw. There were two groups there. There were men wearing JNA helmets and others wearing hats with cockades, and the fact that these two groups were there, side by side, did it not highlight the fact that amongst these fighters, there were differences with respect to what they thought about the communist regime of the past, and didn't it show that some of them preferred to volunteer and to wear a hat with a cockade, rather than wearing a JNA camouflage uniform? Would we be mistaken in thinking that this might have been the reason for this difference we see in the way these fighters are dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true up to a point, but we can't say that there were just two types or three types of fighters. First of all, all of us, as far as the Territorial Defence is concerned, and that's what I'm talking about, we were all issued helmets and uniforms. I, too, had a helmet, but didn't use it. I wasn't duty-bound to use it, so I didn't have it on my head because I wasn't able to put the cockade on the helmet. That's why I wore the cap, the hat. And the other point is this: On the footage, on the photographs, unfortunately, you can see people dressed in different ways, all different kinds of clothing, because there wasn't any discipline or military law to introduce law and order. Had that existed at the time, then probably you wouldn't be harbouring under this confusion and I wouldn't have any trouble in explaining to you who belonged to what unit. The volunteers, at the time in 1991, who went to Vukovar were issued the olive-green uniform in Sid, and weapons too, and then they arrived in Vukovar. They would go to Vukovar, whether in large or smaller groups I'm not sure. But, anyway, it was like this: If they would find a leather jacket somewhere, they'd put it on and throw away the other parts of the uniform. So they dressed whichever way pleased them. They wore whatever they liked, so that they weren't in uniform, as such, they weren't dressed in uniform fashion, and it wasn't easy to distinguish between them, precisely because there was a shortage of uniforms during our operations. We had bands on our shoulders to be able to distinguish ourselves from others. Sometimes we would have these red bands or white bands. When we went into an operation, we would decide, prior to an operation, what we were going to wear, because the Croats noticed we had some bands, so we assumed they might put bands on their shoulders to appear dressed -- to appear as being one of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back to Mr. Seselj and to the time when he went to Vukovar. You gave us a number of details about this, but we heard evidence that Mr. Seselj spoke there. You were there. You met Mr. Seselj. You, yourself, did you hear Mr. Seselj's words, comments? Do you remember or not, or you heard nothing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: I did not come to Mr. Seselj in -- following a regular road; that is to say, Mr. Seselj wasn't ready to deliver a political speech to me. I just happened to be there and asked to be given a cockade. Mr. Seselj said he was sorry, that he hadn't any more cockades on him. And I didn't want to ask a vojvoda to take off his own cockade from his hat, so he ordered one of the security details who was with him to find a cockade, and that's what happened, and he gave it to me. So there was no political discussion. And the second point is I had absolutely no interest in politics at the time. I wasn't interested in listening to talk of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to check with you something which happened, which has been mentioned by some of the witnesses. According to some of the witnesses, and this is the Prosecution's case also, it seems that Mr. Seselj, with the help of a loudspeaker, would have asked the Croats or the Ustasha - this question remains unanswered - to surrender. Was this something you were aware of or does this not ring a bell at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Seselj was over there, I have no knowledge of that. I read about it afterwards in some papers. Unless I'm very much mistaken, I think it was the "Arena" newspaper that published something like that after the liberation. I can't be more specific. I think that Mr. Seselj, on the cover page, was shown walking around in his uniform, something like that, but I really don't know anything about that myself. I read something about it subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in open session, I'll ask the same question, but phrase it differently. On the next day following the events, this is my question, did you refer to your superiors and did you inform them about this? My colleague is calling my attention to this. You don't need to answer this question, because this could potentially incriminate you. Do you wish to answer or do you not wish to answer in public?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I have the option not to answer, then it's better for me not to give an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll discuss the matter with my colleagues to see whether you should answer this or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will move on to another question. As regards the other fighters, you were a member of the Guards Brigade, and the other fighters were members of the TO. When you were on the ground, when you were mopping up the streets, you explained to us what this meant from a military standpoint. Did you have the feeling that you were acting as if this were a military operation that was being conducted by a high-ranking leader?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, while I was in the Territorial Defence, it was explained to me that we were members of the left flank under the command of the Guards Brigade, which means that the main person in command was Colonel Mrksic. And he didn't issue direct orders to my unit, but he did have generalised orders and plans for that particular day, and then the lower-ranking officers would develop that based on the situation on the ground. So I considered that we were constantly under the command of the Guards Brigade. I am actually convinced of that being the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you answered one of the questions put to you by the Prosecutor, you drew my attention to something else. You said that Vukovar could have been taken in one day. These are your own words. And as far as you were concerned, this was -- came to you as a surprise, that the "siege," quote/unquote, of Vukovar lasted quite a long time. And then you added -- when you answered another question you said that the fighters that were Croatian had ran away. So if I put all of these answers together, I ask myself the following question: Were there a lot of Croatian fighters in Vukovar? You were there. What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the Guards Brigade arrived in Vukovar, or, rather, to Negoslavci, as far as I know, before the Guards Brigade, it replaced the Mitrovica Corps, who had the assignment of deblocking the barracks. That was the prior assignment. So the Territorial Defence then or a unit of farmers from Negoslavci launched an operation to deblock the barracks, and they routed all the Croats and reached almost down to the centre. And had the Mitrovica Corps at the time followed that unit of the Negoslavci, whether members of the Territorial Defence or whatever they were, the battle for Vukovar would have been over there and then. But quite simply, the army didn't want to follow them. They arrived at the barracks, stopped there, and didn't go any further, they didn't advance further. So I had the impression that quite simply the army, for some reasons of their own, didn't actually wish to take control of Vukovar at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can also add that at that time, unless I'm mistaken, it was the 1st Zagreb Battalion that defended Vukovar at that time, so actually they were routed and they had no army to speak of after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In November, when these events unfold, you were an educated man, you had some understanding of what was going on. You were acting as a fighter in order to maintain the former Yugoslavia and protect its borders that were the 1945 borders, because at that time Croatia had not been declared independent yet by the European community, or you were a fighter, like your fellow fighters, because you wanted to defend the Republic of Serbia in Vukovar? What was your personal assessment of the situation at the time? Why had you decided to get involved in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I've already said that. I came for a number -- to Vukovar for a number of reasons. The main reason was that I felt duty-bound towards the oath I had taken. That's the first reason. So the reason was that at the time, it was still the SFRY, Yugoslavia by law. The second reason was my nationalist motive as a Serb, because I considered that if my people were fighting somewhere, I had to fight too, with them. There were a number of other reasons as well. My parents were over there. But the first two reasons were the decisive ones which led me to take the decision to go. I didn't decide to do that overnight. I fought a psychological battle with myself for about a fortnight, whether to go to war or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did your superiors share the same views or were their motivations different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if my answer could have disclosed my identity. Perhaps we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, and we are now breaking for 20 minutes. After the break, Judge Harhoff will put a number of questions to the witness. Then it will be up to Mr. Seselj to begin his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. We'll stop at quarter past 1.00. Judge Harhoff has a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I have a small question first regarding Ovcara, and then I have a more -- a question of principle about the command and control that applied to the military operations in Vukovar. But let me just first put my small question relating to Ovcara. My question is that I'm not sure I understood what you told us about the reasons why the detainees were not simply shot. If the plan was to kill them anyway, why were they not just executed by way of gunfire? I'm not sure about the answer that you gave us to this question, so I would like you to explain to us, if you know, why the prisoners in the hangar were not just simply shot dead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I really don't know. I can just tell you what I think. It's an assumption. I really don't know. Would you like me to tell you my assumption? My assumption is that up until the last minute, they didn't know what they would do with the prisoners, and I personally think that they were waiting for a decision from higher up. I don't know if this was from the Krajina government or anything like that. And then when they received a decision in some way, when they received some kind of indication, then they were told what to do. As far as I know, they were waiting for an hour or two before they started with the executions. This is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just to be sure, the executions were committed by way of beating and shooting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all passed through the gauntlet, from what I know. They were not all beaten. Some were beaten, some were not. And later, they were taken away and killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think you told us, but I'm not sure. I think you told us that most of the killing, most of the killing of the detainees or the prisoners, took place inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't think that anyone was killed in the hangar. I didn't see any dead bodies in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right, thank you very much. Let me then move to the more important question that I had regarding the coordination of the operations in Vukovar. And my question is if you were able to form an opinion about how the operation to clean the streets in Vukovar was organised. I think you told us that Colonel Mrksic was in command of the Guards Brigade and maybe also of the operations of the Territorial Defence; I'm not sure. So my question is: How was the operation to take Vukovar organised, in terms of military organisation? And in particular, of course, who controlled the actions carried out by the SRS? Can you give us a picture about how the fall of Vukovar -- how the taking of Vukovar was organised, from a military point of view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way the command was executed was from the Negoslavci headquarters, because Mrksic was there, commanding the Guards Brigade. So that started from his staff, and orders were conveyed via Captain Radic, who was in charge, I think, of coordinating with the Territorial Defence, which was holding the left flank along the action -- axis of the brigade, which means that they were under the command of the Guards Brigade. As for conveying the orders by Captain Radic, there was section and company meetings of the TO at the house of Stanko Vujanovic, where the orders that were received from Negoslavci were reviewed and the plans were drafted for the actions of smaller units on the basis of the orders that were issued from Negoslavci. I doubt that Colonel Mrksic personally issued orders about what each squad should do. He probably issued a general order relating to the left flank and then later plans were made about how the plan would be further implemented. I wasn't present at the meetings, and I heard later from Cetina what they used to do at the meetings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, "from Cetinje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How did the SRS volunteers become involved, and who organised their movements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that. They came on the 16th of October. The unit was organised in Sid and sent to Vukovar, and they were assigned to be under the command of the Territorial Defence. So that means that they were weren't directly under the command of the Guards Brigade. As far as I understood, anyone who was not under military command could not be there. They were not considered a military person. Everybody in the zone of operations had to be under the command of the Guards Brigade. As to how they were under the command, I really couldn't say. I'm not going to talk about individuals who were walking about with weapons. There was no organised group numbering more than a few men that was not under the command of the Guards Brigade. This is how I saw matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So what you're telling us, if I understand correctly, is that JNA troops, as well as Territorial Defence soldiers and also volunteers, including the volunteers of the SRS, were somehow subordinated to the JNA Command in the headquarters of the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you now have the floor, and you have three hours and five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness 002, at the beginning I have to say that I am grateful to you, because yesterday you clarified some matters that were not clear to me and the names of some people that I didn't know about. And in my reactions yesterday, I already said that the Prosecutor showed that footage earlier, with the intention of showing that those people were volunteers and members of the Radical Party. In my cross-examination, I'm going to put questions to you, but I'm will take care that we don't have any reason to move into private session. I'm going to avoid names that could reveal your identity to the public. At the beginning, I would like you to say if there were any reasons pertaining to me or the Serbian Radical Party due to which you requested protective measures.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no such reasons. I asked for protective measures in 1997, or actually 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you had no idea then that one day you would appear as a witness in the proceedings against me; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A number of times, you told us that you were apolitical, that you were not interested in politics, but that at one point you were thrilled by the radical idea and the borders of Serbia, Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica that the Radical Party was propagating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But as an apolitical person, of course you could not avoid the media, radio, television, newspapers, where this idea was elaborated upon, so probably you probably became aware of the fact somewhere that the Serbian Radical Party, already in its programme, stated that it was in favour of a united state that would include all Serbian countries, and we mentioned them -- besides Serbia, we mentioned Bosnia-Herzegovina, Montenegro, Macedonia, Dubrovnik, Dalmatia, Slavonia, Baranja; were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are thinking of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: 1990, 1991, before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware before the war broke out of that. Yes, it did seem ridiculous to me then, but later I took it more seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know about our programme, that we were propagating brotherhood and unity of Orthodox Serbs, Catholic Serbs, Protestant Serbs, atheist Serbs, Muslim Serbs which would live fraternally within the borders of one state; did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At any point, did it occur to you that our efforts for a Greater Serbia implied that all Catholics and all Muslims would be driven out beyond the borders of that state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall hearing anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you think that this concealed our idea, our intention, to drive away all Catholics and all Muslims? Could you perhaps perceive any such intention from any behaviour of mine in 1990 or 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, until you came to Vukovar, I didn't analyse you or wasn't interested in you all that much, since I was personally of the belief that the only form that is good for Yugoslavia, for Yugoslavia to survive as such, would be in the form of a monarchy. So the changing of borders, unless it was in a monarchy, I believed would only lead to some new war in the future. So after 1991, I believed that you, let's put it that way, were the only solution that provided us people from Krajina a chance of having our own life within Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever hear me propagating a monarchy, justifying it, or voice any values of a monarchy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never heard you talking about against a monarchy, but I really never followed politics much or thought about it, so I cannot really say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you must have known that I ridiculed the Crown Prince Aleksandar in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know you did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Prince Aleksandar Karadjordjevic is not important here, is he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is one of the negative things that I noticed about you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, maybe you thought that was silly, but you cannot deny that I persistently kept doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you also deny that I actually tried to cure monarchist-leaning persons of that idea by ridiculing Prince Aleksandar, Crown Prince Aleksandar, and in that way I would combat these feelings of monarchism in those people and would awaken ideas, Republican ideas in them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to answer that. I really didn't follow politics. I did follow your speeches in the Assembly because they were interesting because of your vocabulary and your approach, and you always had a victim, and we always laughed and made jokes about that later. But I was not interested in the political programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. But you liked to watch the showbiz effects of my addresses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which actually was calculated to draw in apolitical persons such as you; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I -- you didn't manage to draw me in. I have a lot of sympathy towards you, but only because you are a great nationalist. But I personally think that you have also some negative qualities, especially because you are not a monarchist, but this is another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, sir. 002, nobody's perfect. I hope that is clear to you, and I have always been in favour of a republic since I was born. I never had any monarchist aspirations, although at the time the Serbian Radical Party was first formed, you will remember that there were some individuals with us who really were monarchists; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally believed when the Serbian Radical Party was formed, that it would be a monarchist party, because I believed that it should carry on and inherit the traditions from the time of the kingdom of Yugoslavia or the kingdom of Serbia, when that was part of the monarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you remember that for the purposes of ridiculing the idea of a monarchy, at one point in January 1992, I travelled to Spain to get in touch with a certain Prince Alex D'Anjou in order to discuss these monarchist ideas? That was when Vukovar was already liberated, and this was reported in the media.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
