utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter. We are going to go back to the gist of your testimony. You explained to us here that in the beginning, you were in the Guards Brigade and you were probably aware of the enormous firepower of the Guards Brigade and the most modern equipment that it had in the JNA at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, can you imagine that instead of this Guards Brigade getting stuck in Vukovar, if it had been sent to an assault, would the Croats have had any forces to stop it before it reached Slavonska Pozega?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that Zagreb would have fallen in a few days. I'm convinced of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Zagreb had a lot of -- a large population, so the soldiers would have gotten lost among those people. But would you agree that the Croats did not have the force to stop such a unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And why would, then, such a brigade be sent to get stuck in Vukovar and in order to take part in street fighting, when that street-to-street fighting --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is going extremely fast. We don't even have time to raise objections when the witness is being asked to speculate. It would be good if a break could be made between question and answers, because then I would have time to object to these questions which have thus been asked and that were calling the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, please try to slow down. Both the witness and yourself are speaking the same language. Our interpreters are doing an outstanding job, but please try to pause between question and answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to respond to the Prosecutor's objection. First of all, both the Prosecutor and the Trial Chamber asked this witness several times to present his views and his assumptions. I hope that I have the same right. Secondly, the Prosecutor has a problem with himself. You know, in all proceedings before any court of law, what is expected is that the counsel for prosecution thinks faster than the accused and to be intellectually superior to the accused. What can I do about it if the Prosecutor is a slow thinker? I put questions very slowly. I paused. I switched off my microphone every time when I would finish. Let them find someone faster, who thinks faster in the Prosecution. What can I do about it? I can't resolve their problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, what we are interested in is the substance of the case, so please go to the essentials, like you started off, and everybody will listen to you carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since you belonged to the Guards Brigade, you should know. Soldiers from the Guards Brigade talked about that, especially members of the military police, that at one point in time before coming to Vukovar, Colonel Mile Mrksic tried to carry out a coup d'etat in the JNA. At one point, he even arrested Army General Veljko Kadijevic, the Minister of Defence, trying to make him resign and hand over to General Blagoje Adzic. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in Sid, I was sent from the staff of the Territorial Defence, as soon as the Guards Brigade arrived there, for a brief training. During the second day of this training, the units of the military police left that area and went to Belgrade. They returned on the following afternoon, something like that. The young soldiers, when I asked them where they were and what happened, they said that that evening they arrested generals and they arrested about 50 generals, that was probably it, and they were supposed to carry out a coup d'etat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, 50 generals is an exaggerated number, but Kadijevic was arrested and a group of his co-workers, but it wasn't 50 of them, because I am a bit better informed about this. However, since that was hushed up in the military and the public never found out about this event, wasn't it obvious that somebody wanted to remove both the Guards Brigade and Mile Mrksic from Belgrade, and they sent them to Vukovar, therefore?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only thing I know is that they had reached some kind of agreement, that they agreed on something. Now, why the Guards Brigade was removed from Belgrade, I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since I was rather informed about the evolving of the Vukovar operation and I have direct knowledge from my conversations with different people, I assume that you should be aware of that and that you should remember that the territorials and the volunteers and politicians from Eastern Slavonia, Western Baranja and Srem, often in their talks, put the question why the JNA was firing with artillery at Vukovar. Do you remember such discussions in the couloirs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you what my conclusion was after the war, and of my friends, too; that Vukovar was totally being destroyed, and on the basis of that, what was being awaited was that the Croats would get recognised by the international public, and that that was the reason why Ovcara happened. As a matter of fact, I have some more assumptions. Now, I just don't know how smart it is for me to say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, so far you've been asked to present your views, so I kindly ask you that when I'm cross-examining you, to act the same way, present your opinion, because you're an inhabitant of Vukovar and a direct participant in the fighting. And to tell you quite honestly, I think that you acted fairly here while giving testimony. I personally have no objections, irrespective of the fact that you mentioned some names that I don't know and some events that I'm not aware of, you know. However, as far as my position here is, I think that your testimony has been fair.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, as far as I managed to find out from talking to others, a certain intelligence group, some kind of Gepard [phoen] or something in Zagreb, I have no idea, was arrested the day after the fall of Vukovar. And the Guards Brigade at that time in the hospital took Njavro, Mrs. Vesna Bosanac, Matos, and a few other doctors and took them to Belgrade, allegedly for interrogations, and they immediately exchanged them for this group of our operatives. Most probably this group of operatives fell precisely in order for this exchange to take place, with mutual agreement. Another thing. An enormous amount of money was left in Vukovar of the SDK, in the safe of the SDK, and it was impossible to open it before an army unit came that knew where the key was, and Dr. Stanovic's wife had the key. They went to see her. They took the key and they opened the safe. The money was collected, and my assumption is, on the basis of some information that I concluded from talking to others, that this money was given to Mr. Jezda to buy marks in Bosnia. So all of this was some kind of a very, very strange game, but I don't know how much this has to do with all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that personally General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, the head of the Security Service of the JNA, was in Vukovar on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was personally in Vukovar, but my personal view is that he is to be blamed for Ovcara. However, I haven't got any evidence. I don't know how smart it is for me to say any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We are going to get to Ovcara, but let me ask you another thing now, from a military point of view. Artillery fire by JNA units, and there were three artillery units of the JNA that were firing at Vukovar, did this have any positive effects, from a military point of view, apart from destroying buildings, that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from a military point of view, if I look at it from the point of view of us, the Territorial Defence, they only impeded us, because if we went out to attack, we had no coordination with them. So we had the most -- were most successful when there were ceasefires, when there was no artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were mortars sufficient to liberate Vukovar, without any kind of artillery, mortars being infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I assume that even mortars were not needed, because when the barracks were deblocked, the Negoslav Detachment completely destroyed the 1st Zagreb Unit, and practically Vukovar was taken in that way, had only the army wanted to follow them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why am I asking you about mortars? A mortar shell, when it explodes, it kills personnel, but it does not destroy buildings, whereas a cannonball destroys buildings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And Vukovar is full of these basements and cellars and firmly built at that, and I think there was supposed to be an atomic shelter under the hospital, so the artillery couldn't really harm these shelters or basements, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably artillery couldn't do anything to them, and I don't think that they used artillery for those shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the top echelons of the JNA used the artillery on purpose in order to destroy Vukovar so that the Croats would have a powerful propaganda weapon against the Serb people and the JNA? Do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, but not fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is being asked to speculate, and I object to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is a relevant one. Please put your question again, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-002, do you agree with me that someone from the top echelons of the JNA ordered on purpose to use artillery to destroy Vukovar so that the Croats would gain a powerful propaganda weapon in the international public against the JNA and the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was this the general view of the inhabitants of Vukovar after November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does the witness agree with me that en masse, the population of Vukovar, I cannot say all of them, but 90 per cent of the population of Vukovar believed and made comments, in their own conversations, that Vukovar was destroyed on purpose, precisely for that reason, to help the Croats attain independence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I can tell you about 50 per cent, because only 50 per cent of the population were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All Serbs in Vukovar thought that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them, 95 per cent of the Serbs for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, any sensible person on the ground knew that this artillery was of no use in fighting and that it was causing damage, irreparable damage. Any person with any common sense understood that; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if this is a statement, is it Mr. Seselj adducing his own evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To avoid any objections, please put the question in a form of a question. Otherwise, the Prosecutor will say that you are testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my question was very clear, concise. On the basis of my own knowledge, I am putting a question to this witness. It is of a bit of a leading nature, but I'm entitled to that. The witness is testifying to facts. I'm asking him whether it's a fact that that is what people in Vukovar thought during operations and after the liberation of Vukovar, and he keeps giving me answers in the affirmative. You can bring in a thousand people from Vukovar who are going to confirm the same thing to you. That is the public opinion of Vukovar. That is why this is fact evidence. That was the public opinion in Vukovar at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, a follow-up question to what has just been asked. Yesterday, I addressed the same issue and I asked you, because you were the one who told us that both the Croats and the Serbs were in the same cellars, and this was quite surprising, since the Serbian artillery was firing. And you responded by saying, yes, the people were down in the cellars together, the Serbs and the Croats. And Mr. Seselj, I believe, is in line with this. I assume that the people who were down in the cellars must have talked to one another, must have wondered why this shooting was taking place, and you yourself said that as far as you were concerned, you found it difficult to understand that situation, since the JNA was in a position to take the town at any time. Therefore, a curious mind might want to understand what lay behind the shooting of Vukovar. There was perhaps a hidden agenda. The idea might have been to draw the attention of the international community on the situation arising in Vukovar. Perhaps this might have a boomerang effect on Croatia and its independence. So you have been to university. I think you are someone that is able to reflect on a number of matters. I don't want you to speculate, but as an academic I would like you to assess the Prosecution's case. What do you think this might be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, all the intellectuals in Vukovar were convinced, in 1991, just before everything happened, that once the army came, everything would be over within a day or two, because they did not see what force could stop the army from entering Vukovar and changing the system, or, rather, bringing back the government organs of the SFRY. So people were wondering. Of course they were wondering, after the liberation of Vukovar, why everything had been destroyed, why the artillery had to be used for shelling the city for two months. However, no one had an answer. Do you realise that? It is so absurd. Quite simply, people could not see an answer. You cannot ask a normal, ordinary person to draw conclusions that were made by some politicians in Belgrade. Mr. Mrksic is a war criminal against the Serbs, as far as I am concerned, personally, because he destroyed -- I mean, in actual fact, Croatia should erect a monument to him and thank him for independence, because had he not ordered the destruction of Vukovar, I don't know what would have happened. Well, perhaps Croatia would have won independence irrespective of that. However, Mr. Mrksic had many other possibilities. What he did was a catastrophe for Serbs, Serbdom and Serbia and the former Yugoslavia, and any form that could have suited the Serbs in any way. I think that I have responded to Mr. Seselj as well, to his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I think that your answer is too categorical. I have to put a question to you. To what extent was Mrksic in charge of commanding the artillery? You must bear in mind that there were three artillery units firing at Vukovar, and not a single one of them was within the Guards Brigade; right? The Guards Brigade was a mechanised brigade. It had two battalions of the military police, it had personnel, it had equipment. It didn't have artillery. The artillery was from the Novi Sad Corps, and I'm not sure, I think there was some from the Kragujevac Brigade, and there was one artillery unit on the other side of the Danube. Do you agree with me that the question has to be put at a higher level; the commander of the 1st Army District, the chief of General Staff, the minister of defence, the chief of the military security service? Don't be so harsh on Colonel Mrksic. He didn't have that power then. Somebody above him had that power; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I don't have much information --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As this question was being put, Mr. Seselj adduces evidence and says who is part of the artillery. For the time being I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, the problem is that Mr. Seselj is putting his questions in the form of a question, because if you look at page 79 and page 90, there are question marks at the end of each sentence, and he says: "Do you agree?" So the witness can say, "I don't know, I disagree, you're making a mistake." In that case, it's a compounded question and a multiple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how the witness can answer all of these questions all at once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please avoid putting many-fold questions. You tend to put complex questions to the witness. When someone is able to take all that in, that's fine, but please try and put shorter questions so that we get shorter answers. But I think he's perfectly capable of answering, so let him answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Mr. Mrksic is indeed a Serb, and if he feels himself to be a Serb, then in my opinion he should have had the officer's honour and duty to do something at the time when he saw what the artillery was doing and he must have known what was happening. He could have handed in his recognition, he could have committed suicide, he could have acted like an honourable Serb officer and arrested all those shits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-002, let's try and take this in a calmer fashion. Let's try and be calm here. I understand that you are revolted by the events in Vukovar because you are a citizen of Vukovar. I'm just trying to look at various levels of responsibility and determine them. I could have committed suicide when I saw what was happening and that the town was being destroyed without any reason. I didn't commit suicide, so perhaps you'll hold that against me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you weren't the TO commander.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he wasn't the immediate artillery commander, but somebody made the decision at the level of the General Staff and 1st Military District and the Ministry of Defence. It was somebody else who made those decisions so that's what I wanted to put to you. But that's not what I'm interested in especially here. I have to let the Judges know that the Prosecutor yesterday received an answer or a response from this same witness, saying that there was a political reason for which the town was totally destroyed, so I'm following on from what was said in the examination-in-chief. And now the Prosecutor's jumping to his feet and making objections. I'm just following on from this. Do you remember, Judges, that was the answer given yesterday, that there was a political reason for which Vukovar was to be totally destroyed? So that's what I want to resolve now, because this is the first, best-placed witness who, if nothing else, can deal with this in a reasonable fashion and reason about it, and he was a citizen of Vukovar, took part in the fighting, and has nothing to do with me and the Serbian Radical Party, except that we met by chance once. And I forgot about that meeting a long time ago, and he's just reminded me of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As we were saying, let's come to the Ovcara question, although we'll go back to what we were talking about earlier. You said you saw two higher-ranking JNA officers there. You said that one was a colonel, and as far as the other, that he had a lower rank. Now, as you were at a certain distance, might you have not been mistaken, because as far as I know, both of them were colonels? Is it possible that I'm right on that score?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible. As I said, I didn't hear the ranks -- see the ranks. I just heard someone address one of them as colonel in the singular so I didn't know what the other one was, but I thought that if he was with a colonel, he might have been a subordinate officer and therefore had a lower rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you happen to realise that nobody had seen those two colonels in Vukovar before; did you realise that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give it any thought. It seems to me amazing that as far as I was able to follow on the internet, the trials conducted about Ovcara and Belgrade, that nobody in the JNA knows anything about it. That seemed to me quite surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that is the problem, because it is a partially-staged trial in Belgrade and then nobody knows anything, whereas I do know about it. I want to receive questions to my specific answers, whereas in my head it is all clear to me. Have no doubts about that. All I want to ask you is whether you ever saw those two colonels in Vukovar before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you what I know about that, and then I'll ask you whether you agree with that or not. The military head of security, General Aleksandar Vasiljevic was reactivated after having retired, or, rather, he reactivated four security officers led by Colonel Bogdan Vujic and sent them to Vukovar to do the dirty work there at Ovcara. Is that possible? Is that how it really happened? Would you say that was possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. The witness is being asked to speculate. He didn't even know what the rank of the second person who was there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, the case relating to Vukovar, well, this Trial Chamber has been seized of this case. When we hand down a judgement, we will have to determine, (a), what happened, (b), who are the people who were responsible. We have learned, since the Prosecution did not tell us, that there is a court case in Belgrade on a particular event, and some people are involved in this case. The accused is telling us that this trial is a staged trial in Belgrade, and is partial. He would like to highlight the fact that these two colonels were sent by a general to go and handle Vukovar. The witness has seen a colonel and a captain, but he's not so sure now, and the accused has evidence about the names of these colonels and he's presenting his case. I don't see why the Prosecution is standing in the way. The Bench cannot only see one side of the story, that of the Prosecution. We also need to hear the case of the Defence and draw our own conclusions. For once, we have a witness who was there at the time, who has seen a certain number of things with his own eyes, so we have to make the most of it. We shall look into the facts, those facts that can be established, and make a difference with what relates to speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only agree with you as far as unravelling the truth is concerned, and I'm just a civil law lawyer. There's no question of just seeing one side of the story, of course. Now, the issue of the trial in Belgrade, I believe that a number of witnesses have already told us that they testified in Belgrade before a court of law. As far as this particular question is concerned, I wonder whether this witness, who has just said that he didn't exactly know what the rank of the second person was, is he the person whom one should put this question to? The question Mr. Seselj is asking is perhaps a relevant question, but I don't know whether this is the right witness. It's not -- on the content of the question, it relates to the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-002, you took part in the fighting in Vukovar sufficiently for you to be able to get to know all the colonels which the Guards Brigade had. Could there have been a colonel hidden away somewhere in the Guards Brigade which you -- whom you hadn't seen before the fall of Vukovar? Would that have been possible at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my case, probably not, because for some reason I knew quite a lot of the officers from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, did you serve the army in that unit? Many did. It's not going to disclose your identity in any way if you answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So we know who, in the Guards Brigade, had the rank of colonel. Colonel Mile Mrksic was one, Colonel Nebojsa Pavkovic. Was there other? The others were lieutenant-colonels, majors, captains, corporals, or whatever; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The chief of the Guards Brigade was Lieutenant-Colonel Miodrag Panic, was he not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I remember, because he presented me with -- you know why I remember? When I visited Vukovar, General Mrksic made a dinner for me at his headquarters in Negoslavci, and we had army beans and sausages. Because everybody joked about the small size of my helmet or my head, Colonel Miodrag Panic gave me his helmet, and then they were laughing because it was the same. And they said it was not the helmet that was too small, it was my head that was too big. So do you remember that I had a helmet on my head when I came to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: I remember your photograph from the papers, and you did indeed have a helmet on your head in that photograph, I think. I'm not quite sure about that helmet, to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you don't have to remember those details, but I remember them because I was a direct participant, of course. But is one fact indisputable, that these colonels -- at least one colonel, and I say that the other man was a colonel, too, whom you saw at Ovcara, you'd never seen before in Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never seen them, period; not only in Vukovar, but I had never seen them at all anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now look at this. We had some victim witnesses here who by chance managed to get away with their lives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this question is of importance. I had no idea what questions Mr. Seselj was going to put to you, but a few hours ago I asked questions about this colonel. If you look at the transcript, you will find that I found it surprising that you mentioned a captain and a colonel without giving their names, and I asked you why you did not give us their names. I thought you were going to answer it was Colonel Mrksic, but you did not say that, so then I wondered who that colonel was. And now it comes out of the cross-examination that there was another colonel who had nothing to do with the organisation in place, someone who would have come from outside. Are you absolutely sure that someone said, "Colonel, Colonel," are you absolutely sure about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quite certain of that, 100 per cent, because they addressed one of them as colonel, they said, "Colonel." As far as the other one is concerned, well, I thought he was a captain, but I'm no longer sure, myself, and of course the possibility does exist that he might have been a colonel too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, possibly you are uncertain because a captain and a colonel has three stars, whereas a colonel has two gold circles round the stars, whereas a captain doesn't. But at a distance of 50 or 100 metres, you can perhaps see the gold stars but not the circles round them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really can't remember. It wasn't that essential, as far as I was concerned. I wasn't focusing on that point. I wasn't thinking about ranks. All I seem to remember is that one was a colonel, so I thought the other one was a captain. Now, why I thought the other one was a captain, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have to tell you that we heard testimony here from some Croats who were incarcerated in Ovcara. They appeared as victim witnesses, and I think that they were fair in their testimony, by and large - I have to say that too - and they saw that these two colonels were drawing up lists of the prisoners in the hangar. Did you happen to notice anything similar, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to their testimony, it was obvious that they came to establish the number of people there and to issue orders about what was to be done subsequently with the prisoners. Was that obvious to you, too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had quite the opposite impression, that they were made to go away from there, sent away from there. But as I say, I wasn't there all the time. I was absent on two occasions for an hour or two, so I don't know what actually went on there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But I remember one thing, and I seem to have made a note of it. When you were asked by Judge Harhoff, you said, in response, that until the very last moment, you didn't know what was to be done with the prisoners; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That means that none of those present, the territorials, the volunteers, the soldiers, nobody had any idea of what was going to happen ultimately to the prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Perhaps Miroljub might have known, as the commander, but the rest of us didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Since we're dealing with people being tried in Belgrade, I'm not going to mention their names at all. Let them prove whether they are guilty, or innocent, or whatever. I'm not going to involve myself in that, meddle in that, but I am interested in certain things to deal with Kameni. We probably won't have enough time to get through that today, so we'll do that tomorrow. But the essential point here, and you can confirm that now, confirm my opinion, my viewpoint, my knowledge and information, that the people who were at Ovcara and took part in beatings -- in the beatings, they wouldn't have done that had they known that the prisoners would be executed subsequently? Do you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't give it any thought previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear the Prosecutor say anything. He sprang up, he was on his feet, but I didn't hear what he had to say, whether he had any objections. Perhaps his chair is giving him some trouble and he's jumping up and down. Perhaps he should be offered another chair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I believe that because of the answer, the objection lost all its value.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you then agree that somebody organised all this at Ovcara in order to have a political effect; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you said that yesterday during the examination-in-chief, you said something similar to that; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I thought I said that. That's my opinion. I don't remember whether I actually expressed it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, very well. Now, in a few words, we're going to deal with another issue -- or, rather, the question of my visit to Vukovar. You've already said that throughout the time, there was shooting from Croatian artillery and that they seemed to be looking for the location I was in, so that means that we were subject to danger; I was, myself, and all the people around me. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was shooting from rifles, automatic weapons, snipers, while I was touring the frontline?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in front at the time, really. I can't remember why, but I went back because of something, so that -- well, I do know because they told me. People told me, the people from my unit, that you were warned not to expose yourself very much because the Ustashas were there and that they might shoot at you, but that you didn't want to listen. Now, I personally don't know anything about snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, but we were exposed to risk and we could have been killed at any moment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, under such conditions and circumstances, was it possible for me to rally around me 50, 100, or more volunteers, territorials, soldiers of the JNA and to deliver a speech to them? Was that possible, even if I had wanted to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that point in time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there any period during my visit to Vukovar where I could have held a rally like that to gather people around me and to hold forth to deliver a speech? Was that at all possible at any time during the visit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you could have done that, I can't say. I didn't hear of anything like that happening. Now, what the possibilities were, the feasibility of it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you probably would have heard if something like that had happened. They would have talked about it, they would have said, "That madman is holding a rally with the snipers firing round about." That would have been the reaction of ordinary people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that most probably I would have heard about it and that I would have attended, because I would have been very interested in hearing what there was to hear, what there was to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Perhaps my question is surprising to you, but we have heard testimony from several false witnesses who claim that I delivered some sort of speech over there. That's why I'm asking you, so that you shouldn't be surprised.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the term "false witnesses" should not be used, and it may influence the answers of the witness. I strongly object to that type of wording being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Seselj, you've mentioned "false witnesses" a number of times. The Chamber has no idea about what the situation is. We'll need to decide about that in due course. Please try to avoid calling people false witnesses. You may be right, but you may be wrong as well, and there's no need to use that sort of language in front of a witness, who may think that he can be regarded as a potential false witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I insist on my right to use those terms. This is a cross-examination, and my freedom is much greater than the Prosecutor's freedom during the examination-in-chief. And, secondly, I have already expressed my position that I believe that the testimony of this witness is very fair, at least in terms of the indictment against me. It is my right to claim that the indictment is false, however, and the Prosecution here is bringing forward false witnesses. I will never give that right up. What you are stating, as Judges, that you have not affirmed yourself of that yet, that is up to you, and it will then depend on the judgement. I, however, don't have anything like that here. I was not afraid in Vukovar, I was not afraid of the bullets, and I'm not afraid of the judgement. So I am actually not going to give up my right to describe them how I wish, but I have not been revealing any particulars about their identity or anything like that, or have not put them in any danger at all. So would you please allow me to continue with my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you will be allowed to continue with your cross-examination. Of course, I can't prevent you from using such-and-such term. I can't prevent you from doing so. The only thing I can do is to tell you that you should not use these words. You've explained at length why you believe that the indictment is a false indictment. You've repeatedly said that some witnesses are false witnesses. We've heard you. We'll have to decide eventually what conclusions should be drawn. But if you keep repeating the same thing, the representatives of the OTP will stand up systematically to object, and we are wasting time. You're dealing with interesting points, and I find that more interesting than a discussion about false witnesses. You have the opportunity to highlight significant points for your case. Please take advantage of that. Get to the point. Highlight your arguments without talking about false witnesses, because if tomorrow you use the same words again, the Prosecutor, this one or another one, will stand up to object, and I again will have to repeat what I'm saying just now. We've been discussing this topic ten times already. You are an intelligent man. You have demonstrated it on many occasions. Please get to the point. That's what we find interesting here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I should add something and tell Mr. Seselj that the Trial Chamber is in a position and can tell him not to use that sort of language. The next time Mr. Seselj uses that sort of language, I'm going to ask the Trial Chamber to make a ruling on that point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can take away my right to my defence, too. That would not be the first time that happens to me. Please keep in mind that nothing can surprise me and I'm prepared for everything, but you may wish -- you may do whatever you wish. However, I did not use anything in my cross-examination that was not permissible according to the Anglo-Saxon system. Let us remember what the cross-examination was like in the famous case of Oscar Wilde. Okay, I'm perhaps not at that level, but perhaps even 100 points higher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a mixed jurisdiction and not a common-law jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. The mixed elements are to my prejudice, I must note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. I can't say anything with respect to the common-law system. Of course, I'm going to look into this matter, but in my own country no accused, no lawyer, can be prevented from saying that a witness is a false witness, but of course he has to prove what he's saying. Now, when it comes to the common-law system, as part of the cross-examination, can one be allowed to say that someone is a false witness? I don't know, I have no idea. My fellow Judge is quite right in saying that we are working here in a mixed system, and we need to look into this matter in the perspective -- from the perspective of the common-law system, from the perspective of the mixed system. If my fellow Judge wants us to look into the matter, we can do so, but Mr. Mundis, who is from a common-law jurisdiction, may be able to shed some light on this for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Of course, the Prosecution, if it would be helpful, would be prepared to brief this issue fully for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. The gist of this type of objection or this type of problem, from what might be considered more of a common-law perspective, is simply that it's argumentative, and in that sense I think the procedural framework in which we operate does borrow a bit from the common law. We save arguments for the end of the case, when all of the evidence is in. It's premature at this stage to be considering any witness's testimony to be false, because the Trial Chamber hasn't heard all of the evidence, and so in that respect we save, in the common law, the argument for the end of the trial when all the evidence is in. Similarly, the Prosecution doesn't stand up and bolster for the credibility of the witness at the end of their testimony. We don't make comments along the way that this witness is truthful or this witness is not. These are matters to be addressed at the end of the case, when the Trial Chamber has heard all of the evidence. Again, we can fully brief this issue if the Trial Chamber would be interested in that, but the gist of it is that in the proceedings here, we save argument until the end of the trial. We don't have a string of ongoing argumentation concerning the evidence that's led on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. What Mr. Mundis is saying is in line with what I said, myself. I said that ultimately, eventually, we would decide whether some of the witnesses had been false witnesses or not. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor. We have eight minutes left for today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Seselj, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just need to remind you that the previous witness, when he testified, you brought him a standby lawyer because the Prosecution established that the witness was lying, but still they did not -- still they brought him forward to testify. But never mind, I still have a couple of questions to finish a topic for today, and then tomorrow we'll discuss some other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti here asked you whether you heard over the sound system if I was calling Ustashas or Croat soldiers, I don't remember which term I used, was calling them to surrender. You said that you didn't hear anything like that. Do you know if, in late September or early October, this was done by the Serb Radio Vukovar, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a radio and some journalist. I think his last name was Stankovic. He was giving reports. I don't know if this was on Radio Vukovar or not. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because I seem to remember that a journalist from Vukovar came to Belgrade for an interview with me. Did you maybe hear this interview with me broadcast on Radio Vukovar at the time when I was not there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did not keep the audiotape of that interview because of the circumstances under which it was broadcast, but I do seem to recall that at that time, I did issue an appeal that the Croatian paramilitaries and the Ustashas should surrender in order to avoid further sacrifices and destruction. This was in late September or early October. But there are witnesses here who have testified and said that they have heard my voice over some sort of loudspeaker, but I don't know if there was a system like that at all. Was there any kind of loudspeaker system set up on the truck that moved through Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the witness very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, sorry, the interpreters are unable to catch what you're saying when you have your hand in front of your mouth, so please speak directly into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I know, representatives of the Guards Brigade, officers, a couple of times did call the Ustashas to surrender over the loudspeaker. I cannot be sure, but I even think that Major Sljivancanin called them to surrender, also using the loudspeaker. I know that they tried to get in touch with Jastreb. They also called him to surrender. But I didn't hear you calling anyone to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did any of the officers who addressed the people over the loudspeaker pronounce the letter "R" in this French way in which I am pronouncing it? Do you seem to recall anything like that, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. These are just details, but they did draw my attention to me that there was an officer who pronounced the sound "R" in a similar way, so perhaps this is where the confusion comes from. Anyway, you said after the war, Stanko Vujanovic became a member of the Serbian Radical Party; after the war, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember when the Serbian Radical Party in Vukovar was founded? According to my information, this was sometime in the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that he did become a member, and later he was given the title of "vojvoda," but I don't know when exactly this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you recall that the president of the Serbian Radical Party in Republika Srpska Krajina was Rade Leskovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He's from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he's somewhere from the outskirts of Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Actually, you're right. He's from Osijek, and then during the war he fled to liberated territory.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that during the war, he was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party and he was the deputy minister for information in the government of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem and that he appeared on television in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I have a very bad opinion of that man because he changed -- switched parties like underwear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what sort of a man he was. I'm talking to you about facts. You cannot dispute the fact that he was the president of the Serbian Radical Party for the entire Serbian Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. May I answer? Look, he was a member of some party before the war, during the war. After the war, he became a radical. I don't know how long he was a radical for. He probably switched parties again, and he probably founded his own party as well. He probably again has a party of his, but I really don't know. I wasn't that interested in him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The only thing that is important to me is that you recall that for a while he was the president of the Serbian Radical Party for the Republic of Serbian Krajina; you do not dispute that. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Stanko Vujanovic in 1993 was a candidate for an assemblyman representing the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that he was an assemblyman candidate. I think that this was in 1993. You probably have the correct information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The first democratic elections in the Republic of Serbian Krajina took part in December of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you know he was elected by a large majority as an assemblyman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what you think about him, what you think about Rade Leskovac, and I'm not voicing my own opinion about them, either. I'm just going over facts here. During the war in Vukovar, did you even hear of anyone enrolling people into the Serbian Radical Party, bringing in application forms and enrolling civilians, soldiers, JNA members, volunteers? Did you ever hear of anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, the answer is, "No." We need to adjourn now. We'll resume tomorrow morning at 8.30. Mr. Seselj, you will have two hours and 20 minutes to complete your cross-examination. We'll resume tomorrow morning at 8.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
